findings.topic: Apple Watch: no built-in standard BLE heart-rate broadcast
findings.detail: Wahoo's support page says the Apple Watch does not send heart rate over standard Bluetooth or ANT+, so apps cannot connect to it directly. Other trainer apps (BitGym, FulGaz) work around this with a relay app such as HeartCast: the watch sends heart rate to the iPhone, and the iPhone re-advertises it as a standard Bluetooth Heart Rate sensor (https://support.bitgym.com/hc/articles/360020716772, https://feedback.fulgaz.com/help/articles/360046977571-can-i-use-my-apple-watch-for-heart-rate). I found no Apple documentation of a native broadcast option in watchOS 26. The only claim is one Zwift forum user (Sept 2025), and it is unconfirmed (https://forums.zwift.com/t/connecting-apple-watch-for-heart-rate/595500).
findings.recommendation: Treat the Apple Watch as a heart-rate source only through a relay app. Do not spend time building your own watchOS or iOS app tonight.

findings.topic: Which Apple Watch relay app to use (checked against the App Store on Oct 17, 2026)
findings.detail: HeartCast (Logic Phase LLC, id1499771124): free, version 3.9.0 updated 2026-10-06, needs iOS 18.6 or later. Its listing says to start a workout on the watch and to 'Ensure HeartCast is visible on your iPhone when connecting'. It says it 'will continue to run in the background during your workout' and that heart rate does not leave your devices, though the app uses Google Analytics and Crashlytics. HR Broadcast (id6766073249): the App Store pages for us, ca, lb and mx return 404, and the iTunes lookup API returns 0 results, so treat it as unavailable. HeartBLE (id6758879454, v1.7, updated 2026-09-30): an app that runs on the watch only and claims to broadcast directly from the watch with no iPhone in between; 7-day free trial, then a one-time purchase. Echo (id1494679144): free workouts are limited to 20 minutes. BlueHeart: last updated 2021-04-29. HeartRateBroadcaster (GitHub): advertises 0x180D/0x2A37 through CBPeripheralManager and sends an update once per second whether or not the value changed. It is free on TestFlight, but sideloading it needs a paid developer account (https://github.com/tankbottoms/HeartRateBroadcaster). None of these listings say they send RR intervals.
findings.recommendation: Use HeartCast as the primary relay because it is free, maintained and works for 'anything that supports a chest strap'. Install HeartBLE (free trial) as a backup on the watch. Test both within the first 15 minutes.

findings.topic: iOS background-advertising pitfall for non-Apple receivers
findings.detail: Apple's Core Bluetooth guide says that when an app advertises from the background, the local name is not broadcast. The service UUIDs move to an 'overflow area' that only scanners looking for those exact UUIDs can find. An Apple forum answer adds that a non-Apple central device cannot decode the overflow area because its format is undocumented (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/814450). An ESP32, or Chrome on Windows/Android, may therefore not find the iPhone relay once HeartCast is in the background. HeartRateBroadcaster also notes that background Bluetooth is not available with free provisioning profiles.
findings.recommendation: Keep HeartCast open on an unlocked iPhone while the receiver scans and connects; once connected, you can lock it. Match the device by service UUID 0x180D or by name, not by MAC address: iPhones use rotating private addresses (this is my inference, not tested). Practise the reconnect before the demo.

findings.topic: Apple Watch update rate and why it cannot give live HRV
findings.detail: Developer forum reports say workout heart rate from HKWorkoutSession / HKLiveWorkoutBuilder updates about every 5 s, even when polled every second (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/724724). Relay apps resend the latest value at 1 Hz. A 2024 forum post reports that the watch does not store beat-to-beat (HKSeriesType.heartbeat) data during a workout (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/746218). Background HRV (SDNN) readings are sparse: about every 2 h during sleep on older watches. watchOS 27 adds a HealthKit RMSSD type, and Series 12 can measure HRV as often as every 5 minutes, but Apple has not confirmed that the watch writes RMSSD samples, and delivery to apps is expected to be closer to hourly than continuous (https://www.themomentum.ai/blog/apple-watch-series-12-ios-27-rmssd-healthkit).
findings.recommendation: From the Apple Watch, show heart rate only, as 'about 1 Hz display, about 5 s underlying samples'. Do not compute or claim RMSSD from it. Label HRV as simulated or roadmap unless a source with real RR intervals is connected.

findings.topic: Fitbit: which models can stream heart rate in real time
findings.detail: Google's support page lists Fitbit Charge 6, Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 2/3/4/5 as able to share heart rate with apps that use the Bluetooth Heart Rate Profile. On the Charge 6: swipe down from the clock face, tap 'HR on Equipment', then once the equipment connects tap Share, then Start. The Charge 6 connects to only one device at a time, and sharing reduces battery life. Google describes the link as 'encrypted Bluetooth', so it may need pairing (https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/fitbit/fitness-tracker-charge-6/). RR intervals are not documented. Users report the feature works with few apps (Strava yes, Zwift and Rouvy no) and that Garmin Edge support broke after a firmware update (https://forums.garmin.com/sports-fitness/cycling/f/edge-1040-series/417427/fitbit-charge-6---hr-broadcasting). Sense and Versa 3 need the third-party 'HR Service' watch app plus an Android companion app; there is no iPhone version, and apps on the same phone cannot connect to it (https://gallery.fitbit.com/details/6503a799-37f7-43bf-8775-23f1742e2a4e). Fitbit said Sense 2 and Versa 4 will not get third-party apps (https://9to5google.com/2023/02/17/fitbit-studio/).
findings.recommendation: Check the exact Fitbit model in its settings now. If it is a Charge 6, use it as a second real heart-rate source and backup through the same Web Bluetooth page, and check bit 4 of the flags byte for RR. If it is any other model, use it only as a vibration channel (see the haptics finding).

findings.topic: Fitbit Web API: do not use
findings.detail: The Fitbit developer site says support for the legacy Fitbit Web API ended on September 30, 2026, and the API will be turned off on October 30, 2026. The intraday endpoint (/1/user/-/activities/heart/date/[date]/1d/1sec.json, scope heartrate) is open to Personal apps. However, data reaches the API only after the device syncs with the phone app, about every 15 minutes while the app is running (https://community.fitbit.com/t5/Web-API-Development/Auto-Syncing/td-p/4816833). Every Google Health API scope is Restricted and needs a privacy and security review (https://developers.google.com/health/about).
findings.recommendation: Skip it. It is too slow (about 15 minutes) for a check-in prompt and will be shut down within two weeks of judging.

findings.topic: Apple Shortcuts / Health Auto Export path
findings.detail: A Shortcut can use 'Find Health Samples' (Heart Rate, sorted by start date, limit 1) followed by 'Get Contents of URL' to POST JSON with a secret header to your backend (https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/build-personal-health-api-shortcuts-serverless/). Shortcuts run on automations or manually, not as a continuous stream, and the watch's HealthKit data has to sync to the iPhone first. Health Auto Export's REST automation needs Premium, and users describe it as 'a bit flaky' because of iOS background limits (https://tzovar.as/exporting-data-apple-health/).
findings.recommendation: Last resort only. Expect delays of minutes. Do not use it for the live demo.

findings.topic: Standard Heart Rate Measurement (0x2A37) format and RR parsing
findings.detail: Byte 0 is a flags byte. Bit 0: heart rate is uint16 little-endian if set, uint8 if not. Bits 1-2: sensor contact supported/detected. Bit 3: a 2-byte Energy Expended field (kJ) is present. Bit 4: RR intervals are present, each a uint16 in units of 1/1024 s, with several possible per notification, oldest first. Notifications arrive about once per second. To convert: rr_ms = raw * 1000 / 1024. Some devices fake RR as 60000/HR; Guy Rutenberg's open-source Web HR Monitor warns when RR stays within 1 ms of 60000/HR (https://www.guyrutenberg.com/2026/04/04/web-hr-monitor-heart-rate-and-hrv-in-the-browser/, code at github.com/guyru/web-hr-monitor, live at guyru.github.io/web-hr-monitor).
findings.recommendation: Always read the bpm width from bit 0 and skip the energy field when bit 3 is set. Only treat RR as real when bit 4 is set and the values are not equal to 60000/HR.

findings.topic: Laptop or Android Chrome Web Bluetooth bridge (fastest receiver)
findings.detail: Web Bluetooth works in Chrome on ChromeOS, Android 6.0+, Mac and Windows 10. It needs a secure context (HTTPS, or http://localhost for development), and requestDevice must be called from a user gesture. Chrome's documented pattern: navigator.bluetooth.requestDevice({filters:[{services:['heart_rate']}]}), then device.gatt.connect(), getPrimaryService('heart_rate'), getCharacteristic('heart_rate_measurement'), startNotifications(), and a 'characteristicvaluechanged' listener. Firefox and Safari do not support it (https://www.guyrutenberg.com/2026/04/04/web-hr-monitor-heart-rate-and-hrv-in-the-browser/). On an iPhone, the separate Bluefy browser (free, iOS 12+) adds Web Bluetooth (https://apps.apple.com/app/id1492822055), but the iPhone running HeartCast should not also be the receiver.
findings.recommendation: Make this the primary receiver. Add a /hr-bridge page to the Next.js app, served on localhost from the demo laptop. Parse each notification and POST {ts, bpm, rr_ms[], source, simulated:false} to FastAPI, which writes to a Tiger Data hypertable. Reconnect on 'gattserverdisconnected'. First do a zero-code check by opening guyru.github.io/web-hr-monitor with HeartCast running.

findings.topic: ESP32 as the receiver (NimBLE-Arduino central plus Wi-Fi)
findings.detail: NimBLE-Arduino (h2zero) ships a NimBLE_Client example and a NimBLE_Secure_Client example (for devices that need bonding, such as a possibly encrypted Charge 6). The main API calls: NimBLEDevice::init(), getScan()->setScanCallbacks(), advertisedDevice->isAdvertisingService(NimBLEUUID("180D")), NimBLEDevice::createClient(), pClient->connect(advDevice), getService("180D")->getCharacteristic("2A37")->subscribe(true, notifyCB) (https://github.com/h2zero/NimBLE-Arduino/tree/master/examples). Espressif lists Wi-Fi station mode alongside a connected BLE link as a supported, stable combination. Wi-Fi and BLE take turns on the shared radio, and BLE scans can be interrupted by Wi-Fi.
findings.recommendation: Stretch goal only. The kit has no confirmed micro-USB data cable, so the ESP32 may not be flashable at all, and PICkachu's time is better spent on squeeze and fall detection. If you try it, scan for UUID 0x180D while HeartCast is in the foreground, and send heart rate to the backend over the same Wi-Fi link that carries squeeze events.

findings.topic: Borrowing a chest strap is the only fast way to real RR and HRV
findings.detail: Garmin watches can broadcast wrist heart rate (Settings > Sensors & Accessories > Wrist Heart Rate > Broadcast Heart Rate; this shortens battery life), although some models broadcast over ANT+ only (https://support.trainerroad.com/hc/en-us/articles/16027042835099-How-to-Use-Broadcast-Mode-to-Sync-Heart-Rate-Data-from-Garmin-Watches-to-TrainerRoad). The phyphox heart-rate logger reads and logs RR intervals from Polar H9 and H10 straps over the Bluetooth Heart Rate Service (https://phyphox.org/wiki/index.php/Polar_H9_or_H10_(Bluetooth_Heart_Rate_Service)). The Polar SDK exposes H10 RR intervals in both ms and 1/1024 s.
findings.recommendation: Ask in the HTV Discord or around the hacker space for a Polar H9/H10 or a Garmin HRM strap you can borrow. The same bridge page would then compute real RMSSD with no code changes.

findings.topic: How to compute RMSSD and how long a window it needs
findings.detail: RMSSD is the square root of the mean of the squared differences between successive RR intervals, in ms. It is the main time-domain measure of vagally mediated HRV. The standard recording length is 5 min. Shorter windows (10 s, 30 s, 60 s, 120 s) have been studied: 1 min of resting RMSSD correlated acceptably with 5 min, but ultra-short values are not interchangeable with 5-min norms, artifacts strongly distort RMSSD, and body position changes it.
findings.recommendation: If real RR is available, compute RMSSD over a rolling 60 s window, and only while the accelerometer shows the wearer is still. Drop implausible RR values (for example outside 300-2000 ms, or more than 20% different from the previous one; these are my suggested cut-offs, not from the paper). Compare against the wearer's own baseline only, and show it as a trend, never as a diagnosis.

findings.topic: Optical PPG modules (MAX30102, MAX30105, Grove ear-clip) on an ESP32
findings.detail: For the MAX30102, install 'SparkFun MAX3010x' from the Library Manager. Wire VIN to 3.3 V, SDA to GPIO21 and SCL to GPIO22 (INT optional). Call particleSensor.begin(Wire, I2C_SPEED_FAST), then getIR() and checkForBeat(irValue); an IR value above about 50,000 means a finger is on the sensor (https://randomnerdtutorials.com/?p=226741). The MAX30102 has been validated on the fingertip (under 2.5% error for HR, HRV and SpO2; https://flore.unifi.it/handle/2158/1255013). On the wrist, movement causes most of the error (https://ore.exeter.ac.uk/repository/handle/10871/35591), and a MAX30101 wrist prototype found that voluntary motion strongly distorted the pulse (https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-558586/v1). A sensor held against the wrist by a scrunchie's elastic is therefore usable at rest at best, and unreliable while dancing. The Grove ear-clip sensor outputs one digital pulse per beat on D2 (5 V typical) and its sample code averages over 20 beats (https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/Grove-Ear-clip_Heart_Rate_Sensor/). None of these are in your kit or on the standard MLH lab list.
findings.recommendation: Not worth it tonight. You already own two better optical sensors (the watches). Mention a sensor built into the scrunchie as future hardware that would need validation.

findings.topic: Buying a sensor locally tonight
findings.detail: The Canada Computers site search for 'max30102' returned 0 results (fetched Oct 17, 2026); its Scarborough store is at 1306 Kennedy Rd (https://www.canadacomputers.com/en/storelocator/show/TD). Creatron's former domain, creatroninc.com, now shows an unrelated gambling page, so I could not confirm the College St store is open. Elmwood Electronics (an online shop) lists a Pimoroni MAX30105 breakout at CAD 26.99 and a SparkFun AD8232 ECG board at CAD 28.99, with pickup unconfirmed (https://elmwoodelectronics.ca/search?q=heart+rate). Amazon.ca Prime Same-Day in the GTA: order by midnight for 4-8 a.m. delivery, eligible items only, $25 minimum (https://www.aboutamazon.ca/news/retail/amazon-expands-same-day-delivery-options-in-key-canadian-cities).
findings.recommendation: Do not shop. Even an Amazon overnight delivery arriving at 4-8 a.m. leaves almost no time to integrate before the 7-8 a.m. submission.

findings.topic: Phone-camera fingertip PPG and webcam rPPG (no wearable)
findings.detail: The open-source richrd/heart-rate-monitor page measures pulse from a fingertip over the phone camera and needs the torch, which its README says works only in Chrome for Android (https://github.com/richrd/heart-rate-monitor). On iOS, a user observed applyConstraints({advanced:[{torch:true}]}) working from iOS 17.5.1, and a WebKit engineer confirmed torch support had been added (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=243075). For webcam face video, pyVHR implements POS, CHROM, ICA, PCA, GREEN, SSR, LGI, PBV, OMIT and MTTS-CAN; POS, CHROM, PCA and SSR performed best (https://github.com/phuselab/pyVHR).
findings.recommendation: Skip. Both need someone to actively hold a finger or face still, which contradicts the 'person can no longer ask for help' premise. At most, mention that the camera-PPG page could act as an 'are you OK?' answer that also records a pulse.

findings.topic: Using the watches' own vibration as the discreet 'are you OK?' buzz
findings.detail: Apple: if the iPhone is unlocked, notifications go to the iPhone instead of the watch; if it is locked or asleep, they go to the Apple Watch, unless the watch is locked or in Do Not Disturb (https://support.apple.com/en-us/108369). WebKit: Web Push for web apps added to the Home Screen (iOS 16.4+, using the Push API, Notifications API and Service Workers) 'show on the Lock Screen, in Notification Center, and on a paired Apple Watch'. The permission request must come from a direct user tap. Fitbit: the tracker vibrates for phone notifications when the phone is within 30 ft (https://support.google.com/googlehealth/answer/14225533). ntfy.sh can push with a single curl (curl -H 'X-Priority: 5' -d 'msg' ntfy.sh/topic); its documented action buttons and vibration patterns are Android-focused (https://docs.ntfy.sh/publish/).
findings.recommendation: Send the pre-check-in buzz as a Web Push from the Next.js PWA added to the Home Screen. Lock the iPhone during the demo so the Apple Watch vibrates. On the Fitbit, enable notifications for that app or for ntfy. Test whether notifications still reach the watch while HeartCast's workout is running.

findings.topic: Why heart rate cannot detect spiking or incapacitation
findings.detail: In about 4,100 Finnish employees, alcohol was linked to dose-dependent increases in sympathetic activity and decreases in parasympathetic activity; acute doses of 0.7-1.0 g/kg raised heart rate and lowered HRV (https://mental.jmir.org/2018/1/e23). GHB overdoses, by contrast, often slow the heart: 38% of 65 Swiss emergency cases and 36% of 88 San Francisco cases had bradycardia, and coma was the main finding. GHB is not on routine toxicology screens, and mixing it with ethanol deepens respiratory and nervous-system depression (https://smw.ch/index.php/smw/article/download/409/406/806). Dancing, anxiety and caffeine also raise heart rate. A change in heart rate can therefore go either way and does not point to any specific cause.
findings.recommendation: Pitch line: 'Heart rate never decides you're in trouble. Alcohol and dancing push it up, sedatives can push it down, so it can't tell us why something changed. A sustained shift from your own baseline only makes StillHere ask "are you OK?" sooner. Help is called only if you don't answer.' Never show words like 'spiked', 'intoxicated' or 'unconscious' in the UI. Use 'unusual change from your baseline, checking in early'.

findings.topic: Clearly labelled simulated fallback (needed anyway under KAZE's 'simulations only' rule)
findings.detail: KAZE requires testing by simulation only, and you cannot ethically produce a real heart-rate anomaly on stage. So the anomaly has to be injected even when the watch stream is real. Mixing real and simulated data without labels would break the rubric requirement to separate what is demonstrated from what is simulated. The fallback described here is a design proposal, not a sourced fact.
findings.recommendation: Build a 'sim' heart-rate source in FastAPI that replays scripted traces: steady about 72 bpm; climb to about 125 bpm while the accelerometer shows the wearer still; drop to about 48 bpm; signal lost. Select it from the operator console. Store every sample with source and simulated=true, show a permanent 'SIMULATED SIGNAL' badge on the dashboard and in the incident log, and keep simulated data out of any baseline. If the watch relay fails on stage, switch sources with one click.

recommended_approach:
PRIMARY PATH (real signal, about 1.5-2 h total). Apple Watch, through the HeartCast relay app (free; the iPhone re-advertises standard BLE Heart Rate Service 0x180D/0x2A37), to a Chrome Web Bluetooth bridge page on the demo laptop, to FastAPI, to a Tiger Data hypertable, to a baseline rule whose only output is an earlier check-in.
(0) Setup, about 15 min. Install HeartCast on the iPhone (iOS 18.6+) and the watch, and install HeartBLE on the watch as a backup (7-day free trial). Start a HeartCast workout and keep HeartCast open on an unlocked iPhone while connecting: a backgrounded iOS app hides its service UUIDs from non-Apple scanners. Check that data flows by opening guyru.github.io/web-hr-monitor in desktop Chrome. That page also shows whether RR is present (it will not be for the Apple Watch).
(1) Bridge, 30-45 min (Marco). A Next.js /hr-bridge page on localhost: requestDevice({filters:[{services:['heart_rate']}]}), then 'heart_rate_measurement', then startNotifications(). Parse the flags byte (bit0 uint16, bit3 energy, bit4 RR in 1/1024 s), POST {ts,bpm,rr_ms[],source:'apple_watch_relay',simulated:false} at about 1 Hz, and auto-reconnect on gattserverdisconnected.
(2) Rule, about 30 min. Take a per-wearer resting baseline (median of 3-5 min). If heart rate stays outside baseline +/- a threshold for 60-120 s while the scrunchie's accelerometer shows the wearer is still, start the 'are you OK?' check-in early: LED/blink challenge on the scrunchie plus a Web Push to the Home-Screen PWA, which the locked iPhone mirrors to the Apple Watch as a vibration. The rule never escalates by itself; escalation still requires no response. State the thresholds as assumptions that need validation.
(3) Fitbit, 10 min. Check the model. If it is a Charge 6, use HR on Equipment, then Share, then Start, and connect with the same bridge page as a second or backup source (one connection at a time; may need pairing; check flags bit 4 for RR). For any other model, use the Fitbit only as a vibrating notification receiver. Do not use the Fitbit Web API: it is turned off Oct 30 2026 and only syncs about every 15 min.
(4) HRV. No Apple Watch path gives real-time RR intervals, so no live RMSSD. Compute RMSSD over a rolling 60 s window only if a source has bit 4 set and the RR values are not 60000/HR fakes; for example, borrow a Polar H9/H10 or Garmin strap from another hacker. Otherwise label HRV 'simulated / roadmap'.
(5) Stretch, only if a micro-USB data cable turns up and the squeeze/fall firmware is done: an ESP32 NimBLE-Arduino central that subscribes to 0x2A37 and forwards over the same Wi-Fi link.

SIMULATED FALLBACK (build it regardless, about 20 min). A backend 'sim' heart-rate source replaying scripted traces (steady, a climb while still, a drop, signal lost). Every sample is stored with simulated=true, and a permanent 'SIMULATED SIGNAL' badge shows on the dashboard and in the incident log. One click switches to it if the relay fails. KAZE requires simulation for anomaly scenarios anyway: the live watch proves the data path is real, and the anomaly itself is injected.

DO NOT spend time on: buying a MAX30102 (no local stock found; Amazon overnight arrives 4-8 a.m.), a custom watchOS or iOS app, Shortcuts or Health Auto Export (minutes of delay), or camera/webcam rPPG.

HONEST FRAMING for judges. Demonstrated: a live heart-rate stream from a watch the wearer already owns, and a check-in rule that changes timing only. Simulated: the anomaly, and HRV (unless real RR is connected). Assumptions: the relay app stays connected once started; heart rate refreshes about every 5 s; the watch is worn snugly. Needs validation: thresholds and false-prompt rate, wrist optical accuracy while dancing, and behaviour across individuals. Heart rate is non-specific: alcohol raises it and lowers HRV, GHB slows it in about 36-38% of emergency cases. So StillHere never claims to detect spiking or incapacitation; a heart-rate change only makes it ask sooner, and contacts see nothing until an alert.

findings.topic: Reference fall algorithm built on ADXL345 interrupts (Analog Devices AN-1023)
findings.detail: AN-1023 (Ning Jia) uses four checks: weightlessness, impact, motionless and changed orientation. The register settings in its Table 1 are: BW_RATE 0x0A (100 Hz); DATA_FORMAT 0x0B (±16 g, full resolution); THRESH_FF 0x0C (0.75 g); TIME_FF 0x06 (30 ms); THRESH_ACT 0x20 (2 g, dc-coupled) for impact; THRESH_INACT 0x03 (0.1875 g, ac-coupled); TIME_INACT 0x02 (2 s); ACT_INACT_CTL 0x7F; INT_ENABLE 0x1C (activity, inactivity, free-fall); INT_MAP 0x00. The timing rules are: (1) impact must come within 200 ms of FREE_FALL; (2) inactivity must come within 3.5 s of impact; (3) a fall is valid if the stable reading differs from the pre-fall reading by more than 0.7 g; (4) after that it re-arms with THRESH_ACT 0.5 g (ac) and TIME_INACT 10 s, and 10 s of no movement gives a 'critical' alert; (5) FREE_FALL lasting 300 ms (two FF interrupts less than 100 ms apart count as one), about a 0.45 m drop, gives a 'critical free-fall' alert. It was tested on 80 belt-worn trials (forward, backward, left, right; 20 each), and all were detected. The note itself says 'a more comprehensive, effective, and long-term experimentation is required'. The PDF read here is a mirror; Analog Devices' own copy is at https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/application-notes/AN-1023.pdf, which returned 503 for us.
findings.recommendation: Use AN-1023's four-stage structure and timings as the starting fall detector, computed in software from FIFO samples. Keep the ADXL345 interrupts as a second, hardware signal. When the post-impact stillness and orientation-change checks pass, request an earlier check-in. Never treat it as an alert. AN-1023's 10 s 'critical' rule should only raise the check-in's priority.

findings.topic: ADXL345 register semantics, scale factors and limits
findings.detail:
From the ADXL345 datasheet (Rev 0):
- THRESH_ACT, THRESH_INACT and THRESH_FF use 62.5 mg/LSB.
- TIME_FF uses 5 ms/LSB. The recommended free-fall settings are 300–600 mg (0x05–0x09) and 100–350 ms (0x14–0x46). The free-fall check uses the root-sum-square of all axes, all axes always participate, it is always dc-coupled, and its timer maxes out at 1.28 s.
- TIME_INACT uses 1 s/LSB (maximum 255 s). Inactivity runs on filtered output data, while activity, free-fall and tap run on unfiltered data, so a hardware event may not be visible in the output samples.
- In ac-coupled mode, activity and inactivity compare against a reference value captured at the start of detection. In dc-coupled mode they compare raw values against the threshold.
- Reading INT_SOURCE (0x30) clears the activity, inactivity and free-fall bits.
- Full resolution is 3.9 mg/LSB. Noise is below 1.0 LSB rms on x/y and below 1.5 LSB on z at 100 Hz. Typical 0 g offset is ±40 mg on x/y and ±80 mg on z; offset registers OFSX/OFSY/OFSZ use 15.6 mg/LSB.
- I2C runs at up to 400 kHz. The address is 0x53 with SDO/ALT ADDRESS grounded and 0x1D when it is high.
- Current draw is 145 µA at 100 Hz and 100 µA at 50 Hz (Table 6).
- The FIFO holds 32 samples, with bypass, FIFO, stream and trigger modes.
findings.recommendation: Configure at ±16 g with FULL_RES (4 mg/LSB) so a 7 g impact does not clip. Use 100 Hz. Remove the per-unit offset with a static calibration: a 40 mg bias is roughly 2.3° of tilt error, which matters for head-drop. Read INT_SOURCE once per loop and keep the bits, because reading it clears them.

findings.topic: FIFO burst-read pitfall with the Adafruit library
findings.detail: The datasheet says FIFO entries must be read with multi-byte (burst) reads: 'If a single-byte read operation is performed, the remaining bytes of data for the current FIFO sample are lost.' It also recommends a multi-byte read of DATAX0–DATAZ1 (0x32–0x37) so the axes cannot change between reads. Adafruit_ADXL345_Unified::getEvent() calls getX(), getY() and getZ() one after another (three separate 16-bit reads) and scales by ADXL345_MG2G_MULTIPLIER 0.004 × 9.80665 into m/s^2. With FIFO in stream mode, that pattern would split samples. Adafruit's setRange() always sets FULL_RES (format |= 0x08).
findings.recommendation: Use Adafruit_ADXL345_Unified for begin(0x53), setRange(ADXL345_RANGE_16_G), setDataRate(ADXL345_DATARATE_100_HZ) and writeRegister()/readRegister(). Read samples with your own 6-byte Wire burst from 0x32, repeated FIFO_STATUS(0x39)&0x3F times. Do not use getEvent() once the FIFO is enabled.

findings.topic: Arduino libraries: Adafruit vs SparkFun vs Seeed Grove
findings.detail: Adafruit_ADXL345 provides setRange/getRange, setDataRate/getDataRate, getEvent, getX/Y/Z, writeRegister/readRegister, ADXL345_DEFAULT_ADDRESS 0x53, and register macros such as ADXL345_REG_THRESH_FF and ADXL345_REG_FIFO_CTL. It has no interrupt helpers. The SparkFun ADXL345 library (SparkFun_ADXL345.h) provides powerOn() (which calls Wire.begin() and writes POWER_CTL=8), readAccel() (raw counts), setRangeSetting, setRate, setFullResBit, setActivityThreshold, setInactivityThreshold, setTimeInactivity, setActivityXYZ, setInactivityXYZ, setActivityAc, setInactivityAc, setFreeFallThreshold, setFreeFallDuration, setImportantInterruptMapping, ActivityINT, InactivityINT, FreeFallINT, getInterruptSource() and triggered(). Its arguments are raw register counts clamped to 0–255 (62.5 mg, 1 s or 5 ms per LSB). It has no FIFO methods. Seeed's Grove demo (Seeed-Studio/Accelerometer_ADXL345) uses setActivityThreshold(75) (about 4.7 g), setFreeFallThreshold(7) (about 0.44 g, comment '5–9 recommended') and setFreeFallDuration(45) (225 ms, comment '20–70 recommended').
findings.recommendation: Use the SparkFun library if you want named interrupt helpers. Call Wire.begin(21,22) and Wire.setClock(400000) yourself first. Otherwise use Adafruit plus raw writeRegister() calls with the AN-1023 register values. Either way, run the decision logic in software on FIFO data.

findings.topic: ESP32 wiring, I2C and Grove module constraints
findings.detail: Arduino-ESP32 Wire.begin(sdaPin, sclPin, frequency): on a generic ESP32, SDA defaults to GPIO21 and SCL to GPIO22. setClock() sets the bus speed, and setTimeOut() defaults to 50 ms. The Seeed Grove 3-Axis Digital Accelerometer (±16 g) runs on 3.0–5.5 V and its examples use I2C address 0x53. Seeed's listing describes a 4-pin Grove interface (VCC, GND, SDA, SCL), so INT1/INT2 are not on the Grove cable (https://core-electronics.com.au/grove-3-axis-digital-accelerometer-16g-seeed-studio.html).
findings.recommendation: Wire Grove-to-female-jumper as VCC→3V3 (keeps the I2C levels at 3.3 V), GND→GND, SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22. Assume there is no INT pin and poll FIFO_STATUS and INT_SOURCE every 100 ms. At 100 Hz the 32-deep FIFO fills in 320 ms, so no blocking Wi-Fi call may hold the sensing loop longer than about 250 ms. Run sensing in its own FreeRTOS task.

findings.topic: Sampling rate
findings.detail: A wrist-oriented smartwatch feasibility study sampled at 50 Hz and cites literature that '20 to 40 Hz is enough to properly characterize the human mobility' for fall detection. It also states that 'vigorous motion of the hands may be easily misinterpreted as falls'. AN-1023 used 100 Hz. The Linux kernel ADXL345 driver documentation says the ODR for activity, inactivity and free-fall detection should be 12.5–400 Hz, and recommends a 300–600 mg free-fall threshold (https://docs.kernel.org/iio/adxl345.html). Suffoletto's alcohol-gait study also sampled at 100 Hz.
findings.recommendation: Sample at 100 Hz (BW_RATE 0x0A), so a 30–60 ms free-fall phase spans 3–6 samples and the impact peak is not missed. Compute features on the ESP32 and send 1 Hz summaries.

findings.topic: Published impact and free-fall thresholds (trunk)
findings.detail: Laguna et al. (ICSOFT 2010) summarise Bourke et al. 2007 (trunk tri-axial accelerometer). The upper fall threshold was the lowest peak seen in simulated falls and the lower fall threshold the largest of the low troughs, giving 3.52 g and 0.41 g. Normal activities 'usually produced accelerations of 1 to 2.5 g', although running or sitting can exceed this. Citing Chen et al. 2005, they report a typical fall impact of about 7 g, against less than 3 g (about 2.6 g) when sitting down.
findings.recommendation: For the trunk or head the defensible impact band is 2.8–3.5 g of SVM, with a pre-impact trough of 0.4–0.75 g. Keep ±16 g range because real impacts reach about 7 g.

findings.topic: Real-world performance and false alarms of threshold algorithms
findings.detail: Bagalà et al. 2012 tested 13 published algorithms on 29 real-world falls. Mean sensitivity was 57.0% ± 27.3% (maximum 82.8%), far below the figures reported on simulated falls. The authors state that 'thresholds are usually calibrated on simulated fall signals and are not suitable for real-world fall signals.' Bourke's single thresholds (UFT 1.79 g, LFT 0.73 g in that implementation) produced about 61–65 false alarms in 24 h. Bourke3 had the best trade-off: LFT 0.65 g, UFT 2.8 g, vertical velocity -0.7 m/s, and 'lying' if posture was over 60° for more than 75% of t+1 to t+3 s. It reached about 83% sensitivity and 97% specificity with about 5 false alarms a day, but missed low-impact falls onto beds or sofas. Kangas2 marks the start of a fall when SV drops below 0.6 g and requires impact within 1 s. Kangas's posture check uses the 0.4 s average of the low-pass vertical signal 2 s after impact (0.5 g or less means lying). PPV across algorithms was low (19.3% ± 9.7%).
findings.recommendation: Use this paper to justify the core rule to judges: even the best threshold detectors generate several false alarms a day and miss soft falls, so a motion trigger can only start an earlier check-in. Add a posture and stillness gate (Bourke3 or Kangas style) to cut false triggers.

findings.topic: Wrist placement is the weakest site; dancing and jumping
findings.detail: Quadros-style wrist optimisation on UMAFall (17 subjects, 208 falls, 20 Hz): the smallest wrist impact peak across all falls was 2.5 g. The thresholds tested were 2.5, 3.0 and 3.093 g (median from simulated annealing), and the threshold search 'did not show a clear advantage' over the original 3 g. Impact end is the last sample above 1.5 g, and peaks are searched over the previous 2500 ms. Secondary summaries of Kangas 2008 report sensitivity of 76–97% at the waist, 47–98% at the head and 37–71% at the wrist (https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/16/8/1161, secondary). We found no study that tests dancing directly. Jumping physically reproduces the free-fall-then-impact signature (AN-1023: near 0 g in free fall), so a dance floor will generate free-fall-plus-impact candidates. What separates a real fall is the 2 s post-impact stillness and the orientation change.
findings.recommendation: Use 3.0 g in wrist mode. Add a 'dance context': if ENMO has been at or above 100 mg for more than 60 s, raise the wrist impact threshold to 4 g and require 3 s of post-impact stillness. Always keep the post-impact stillness gate, because a dancer who keeps moving never satisfies it. Record your own dance and jump traces to measure the nuisance rate, and do not claim a dancing specificity figure.

findings.topic: Commercial auto-escalation false alarms (argument for check-in-first)
findings.detail: After Apple's 2022 Crash Detection launch, it fired on roller coasters. Summit County, Colorado logged 71 automated crash notifications from skiers' iPhones and Apple Watches in one weekend, and none was an emergency. Apple shipped 'Crash Detection optimizations' in iOS 16.1.2 and watchOS 9.2. A Japanese fire department logged 134 false alarms between Dec 16 and Jan 23 (https://www.phonearena.com/news/iPhones-crash-detection-feature-is-trolling-the-Japanese-emergency-services_id145240). A long-term real-life fall sensor study found 12/15 falls (80%) at 0.049 false alarms per usage hour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25138139/).
findings.recommendation: Put this in the safety and reliability part of the pitch: well-funded motion detectors still produce false emergency calls in high-energy settings. StillHere never escalates on motion alone. Escalation needs a missed check-in, and the countdown runs on the server.

findings.topic: Apple Watch the team owns: built-in Fall Detection can place a real call; its API is gated
findings.detail: After a hard fall the watch taps the wrist, sounds an alarm and shows an alert. If the wearer is immobile for about a minute, a 30-second countdown starts, then the watch automatically calls emergency services and later messages the emergency contacts. For ages 18–55 setting up a new watch on watchOS 8.1 or later, 'Only on during workouts' turns on automatically. It can be turned off on the watch (Settings > SOS > Fall Detection) or in the iPhone Watch app (My Watch > Emergency SOS). Third-party access to Apple's fall events (CMFallDetectionManager) needs an Apple-granted entitlement, com.apple.developer.health.fall-detection, requested by the account holder (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coremotion/cmfalldetectionmanager).
findings.recommendation: Turn off Fall Detection on any Apple Watch worn during simulated falls or demo runs, or take it off. KAZE forbids real emergency calls, and a demo fall plus a still presenter could trigger one. Don't plan on CMFallDetectionManager tonight. Use the watch for heart rate and as the haptic 'are you OK?' channel through mirrored phone notifications.

findings.topic: Tilt and pitch maths with an accelerometer only (no gyroscope)
findings.detail:
NXP/Freescale AN3461 (Rev 6) gives several pieces.
- Roll and pitch (aerospace sequence): tan(phi) = Gpy/Gpz (Eq. 25) and tan(theta) = -Gpx/sqrt(Gpy^2+Gpz^2) (Eq. 26). Implement roll as ATAN2(Gpy, Gpz).
- The stable roll form is tan(phi) = Gpy/(sign(Gpz)·sqrt(Gpz^2 + mu·Gpx^2)), with mu = 0.01 (Eq. 38), which avoids the singularity when an axis lines up with gravity.
- The angle between any two accelerometer readings is cos(alpha) = (a·b)/(|a||b|) (Eq. 45).
- The method is valid only 'in the absence of linear acceleration'.
- 'All accelerometers are completely insensitive to rotations about the gravitational field vector', so yaw cannot be measured.
findings.recommendation: In hair mode, don't rely on Euler angles, because the module's mounting orientation in a scrunchie is arbitrary. Calibrate an upright reference vector g_ref and compute the head-drop angle as the Eq. 45 angle between low-passed gravity and g_ref. Update the angle only when the reading is quasi-static (| |a| - 1 g | < 0.1 g). Angular rate is estimated from tilt change over 200 ms during quasi-static periods only.

findings.topic: How far people flex the head for phones vs maximum flexion
findings.detail: Lee, Kang & Shin (Ergonomics 2015) had 18 participants text, browse and watch video while sitting and standing. Head flexion was 33–45° from vertical (50th percentile), and texting while sitting gave the largest flexion. In 300 healthy 18–29-year-olds, active cervical flexion averaged 57.7° ± 8.2° (digital goniometer, AAOS method; https://avesis.iku.edu.tr/yayin/e6a38307-12a9-4526-9d9f-efa478dba5e1/normative-values-for-cervical-and-lumbar-range-of-motion-in-healthy-young-adults).
findings.recommendation: A fixed 45° threshold would fire on every phone user. Calibrate each wearer's phone-viewing angle and set the head-drop threshold at max(theta_phone + 15°, 50°). Also require stillness and a minimum hold time, because looking at a phone involves continuous small movements and periodic head lifts.

findings.topic: Head-drop / nodding-off signatures (design precedents, not validated cut-offs)
findings.detail: US10964190B2 (alertness glasses with an accelerometer in the stem) low-pass filters the gravity-direction axis at about 2 Hz. It counts a head drop when that axis falls below a threshold, counts only drops longer than 0.2 s, and also tallies drops longer than 0.5 or 1 s. It escalates from LED to buzzer to a message to nearby devices. US7209569B2 (earpiece with an inertial sensor) says falling asleep shows 'more oscillation before coming to rest in a downward position'. Its example: a user 'gradually nods their head, catches themselves momentarily, continues to gradually nod'. It contrasts this with a 'short and controlled' affirmative nod, and lists time, speed and size of movement as discriminators (https://patents.google.com/patent/US7209569B2/en). An IMU driver-drowsiness study reported 70% success and no validated angular-velocity threshold.
findings.recommendation: Use three head-drop triggers, each only an early check-in: (a) sustained forward flexion beyond threshold with low motion for at least 20 s; (b) a bobbing pattern of 3 or more drop-and-recover cycles within 2 min; (c) a fast drop (at least 25° within 0.5 s) into sustained flexion. Present the 2 Hz low-pass and 0.2 s minimum as design precedents, not validated thresholds.

findings.topic: Head-level acceleration during walking is smoothed and contaminated by head movements
findings.detail: A behind-the-ear sensor (ADXL335 ±3 g, 50 Hz) showed larger errors at slow speeds 'due to sudden head motion while talking or looking around'. The same paper notes that head-mounted sensors give 'smoother oscillations of higher power at low frequencies' than trunk sensors. Menz, Lord & Fitzpatrick (Gait Posture 2003, 30 young adults) found that pelvis accelerations rose on an irregular surface while head accelerations were unaffected (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12855299/). The head actively attenuates sway.
findings.recommendation: In hair mode, expect sway to be attenuated and noisy. Compute sway only during detected straight-walking bouts and use a personal baseline. Treat it as the weakest of the three motion triggers. In wrist mode, turn lateral-sway RMS off: arm swing dominates, and the literature is trunk-based.

findings.topic: Alcohol and gait from a body-worn accelerometer (sway evidence)
findings.detail: Suffoletto et al. (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2020): 22 recruited and 17 analysed, phone on the lower back, 100 Hz. They walked 10 steps out and 10 back each hour after dosing toward a BrAC of 0.20%, with 1-s windows at 50% overlap. Per-participant logistic regression classified BrAC above 0.08% with 92.5% accuracy against a naive 88.2% (sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.92, PPV 0.77, NPV 0.97). The top features were mean amplitude and variance of the x (mediolateral) axis, 'i.e., gait sway'. Population-level models 'were not accurate', and the authors say an application 'would need to collect individual gait measures during sober and drinking periods'.
findings.recommendation: Use a personal sober baseline and present sway only as 'gait looks unusual for you'. Never present it as intoxication detection, which matches KAZE's no-diagnosis rule. Cite this as the reason for per-user calibration.

findings.topic: Defensible sway threshold: reliability (SDD) and speed normalisation
findings.detail: In 35 healthy adults (23–79 years, L3–L4 sensor, 100 Hz, 1-week retest), mediolateral acceleration RMS had ICC 0.83 and smallest detectable difference (SDD) 41.1%. ML RMS ratio (RMSR) had ICC 0.81 and SDD 26.0%, and walking speed had SDD 13.4% (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5017322/). Sekine et al. 2013 define RMSR as directional RMS divided by resultant-vector RMS. In healthy subjects, RMS in all directions was related to walking speed, but ML RMSR was not (rs = -0.10, p = 0.54). ML RMSR was higher in hemiplegic patients (p < 0.01).
findings.recommendation: Day-to-day noise in raw ML RMS is about ±41%, so 2.5× baseline (+150%) is far outside normal variation. It is a conservative, high-specificity tier but probably insensitive, and raw RMS also rises with walking speed. Use speed-normalised ML RMSR as the primary feature. Trigger an early check-in when, over 3 consecutive 4-s walking windows, RMSR is at least the baseline mean + 3 SD and at least 1.26× baseline, and ML RMS is at least 1.5× baseline. Keep 2.5× ML RMS as a 'strong' tier that shortens the check-in further. Say plainly that these are engineering choices derived from reliability statistics, not validated impairment cut-offs.

findings.topic: Prolonged stillness: sustained-inactivity rule from wrist accelerometry
findings.detail: van Hees et al. (PLoS One 2015) used a GENEActiv at 85.7 Hz and ±8 g. They computed arm angle = atan(az/sqrt(ax^2+ay^2))·180/pi from 5-s rolling medians, averaged per 5-s epoch, and defined sustained inactivity as no change larger than 5° for at least 5 min. Against polysomnography (n = 28), 5 min/5° gave sensitivity to sleep 91% ± 13% but specificity to wake only 45% ± 23%. 10 min/5° gave 81% and 60%, and 15 min/5° gave 73% and 65%. Quiet wakefulness often looks the same as sleep.
findings.recommendation: During an active session, flag prolonged stillness when no 5-s epoch angle changes by more than 5° for 10 min (wrist) or 10 min (hair). Shorten this to 3 min if a fall, head-drop or sway flag fired in the last 30 min. Because specificity to wake is only 45–65%, stillness can only prompt a check-in. It cannot tell sleep, calm sitting and unconsciousness apart.

findings.topic: Activity-intensity context (ENMO cut-points)
findings.detail: A 2025 review table lists Hildebrand 2017 wrist/hip ENMO thresholds averaged over 5-s epochs: sedentary below 45 mg, light 45–100 mg, MVPA 100 mg or more (ENMO = max(0, |a| - 1 g)). Another source notes these lab-derived sedentary thresholds 'demonstrated low accuracy' in free-living data (https://researchonline.ljmu.ac.uk/id/eprint/8357/1/Accepted%20Version%20JSAMS%20Sedentary%20Time.pdf).
findings.recommendation: Use ENMO only for context: at or above 100 mg for 60 s or more switches on 'dance context' (stricter fall gate); below 45 mg is required as well as the angle rule before stillness counts. Don't present ENMO as a safety threshold.

findings.topic: Gravity-based orientation-independent vertical/horizontal split
findings.detail: An accelerometer measures gravity plus linear acceleration, and for orientation it is the direction of gravity that matters (Kok, Hol & Schön, inertial sensors tutorial). AN3461 likewise says tilt is valid only without linear acceleration. A low-passed gravity estimate gives the vertical axis. Projecting the dynamic acceleration onto it gives vertical acceleration, and the remainder is the horizontal plane, where the main walking axis (AP) can be found by PCA.
findings.recommendation: In both modes compute d = a - g_lp (g_lp: first-order low-pass at about 0.3–0.5 Hz), v = d·ĝ, h = d - vĝ. Over each 4-s window run a 2×2 PCA on h: e1 ≈ AP, e2 ≈ ML. This avoids depending on how the scrunchie sits in the hair.

findings.topic: FSR hardware for the squeeze input
findings.detail: Ohmite FSR01CE: actuation under 20 g (force to reach 10 MΩ), linear region (log/log) up to 5 kg, 39.70 × 39.70 mm active area, -20 to +85 °C. Ohmite says FSRs suit detecting a change in force, not accurate weight measurement (https://www.digikey.ph/en/products/detail/ohmite/FSR01CE/9178296). Adafruit wires the FSR to power with a 10 kΩ pulldown to ground and reads the midpoint, which also works at 3.3 V. Sensors vary by about 10%. SparkFun suggests about 3.3 kΩ for a broad 0.1–10 kg range (https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/force-sensitive-resistor-hookup-guide/example-hardware-hookup).
findings.recommendation: Wire 3V3 to FSR to ADC pin, with 10 kΩ to GND (try 4.7 kΩ if a hard squeeze saturates). The scrunchie's elastic pre-loads the FSR, so use a rolling idle baseline and calibrate thresholds per wearer relative to that baseline, never as absolute voltages.

findings.topic: ESP32 ADC choice for the FSR when Wi-Fi is on
findings.detail: Older ESP-IDF docs say the application can use ADC2 only when the Wi-Fi driver is not started, and adc2_get_raw() fails between esp_wifi_start() and esp_wifi_stop() (https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/v3.1.5/api-reference/peripherals/adc.html). The current oneshot driver says 'ADC2 is also used by Wi-Fi' and arbitrates access between them (https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/api-reference/peripherals/adc/adc_oneshot.html). Arduino-ESP32 analogReadMilliVolts() returns a calibrated millivolt value, and on ESP32 ADC_11db covers 150–3100 mV.
findings.recommendation: Put the FSR on an ADC1 pin (GPIO32–39, for example GPIO34). Read it with analogReadMilliVolts() at 100 Hz with 11 dB attenuation, so Wi-Fi can never block or corrupt squeeze input.

findings.topic: Timing constants for press, double-press and long-press
findings.detail: AOSP ViewConfiguration.java: DEFAULT_LONG_PRESS_TIMEOUT = 400 ms, DOUBLE_TAP_TIMEOUT = 300 ms (first up to second down), DOUBLE_TAP_MIN_TIME = 40 ms, TAP_TIMEOUT = 100 ms, DEFAULT_MULTI_PRESS_TIMEOUT = 300 ms. Windows' default double-click time is 500 ms, and any value above 5000 ms is clamped to 5000 ms (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-setdoubleclicktime). Ganssle measured mechanical switch bounce at 1557 µs average and 6200 µs maximum, with one outlier switch at 157 ms (https://www.ganssle.com/debouncing.htm). An EE Journal author uses 20 ms as a default debounce (https://eejournal.com/article/ultimate-guide-to-switch-debounce-part-4).
findings.recommendation: Phone defaults (300–500 ms gaps, 400 ms long press) suit sober, practised fingers. For a squeeze that may be slow or impaired, use a 30 ms debounce, ignore presses under 80 ms, treat 80–1000 ms as SHORT and 1000–5000 ms as LONG, and treat anything over 5000 ms as a pressure artifact (leaning on the hair). End a sequence after 1000 ms with no new press, configurable from 600 to 2000 ms.

findings.topic: Accessibility of time limits and impaired reaction time
findings.detail: WCAG SC 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable) says the user should be able to adjust a time limit to at least 10× the default, or be warned and given at least 20 s to extend it. Its example: if 15 s is allowed to respond and hit a switch, 150 s would be sufficient. A small study (8 men) found visual reaction time rose from 294 ms to 459 ms at 0.40 per mille breath alcohol (https://sk.pf.jcu.cz/artkey/stk-201603-0018_vliv-alkoholu-na-zmenu-reakcni-doby-u-muzu.php). That is weak evidence, but it points the same way.
findings.recommendation: Make the challenge-response window 10 s by default and configurable to 30 s. Allow one retry. On the server, missing the squeeze window counts as 'no response so far'. The server countdown is the safety net, not the squeeze timer.

findings.topic: Wi-Fi streaming latency and privacy-preserving storage
findings.detail: Arduino-ESP32 defaults to WIFI_PS_MIN_MODEM (modem sleep). Received data can then be delayed by up to the DTIM period, and WiFi.setSleep(false) gives the lowest latency at higher current (about 145 mA versus 80–108 mA measured on a DevKit). Tiger Data/TimescaleDB add_retention_policy('table', drop_after => INTERVAL '...') drops hypertable chunks older than the interval, with one policy per hypertable (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/api/latest/data-retention/add_retention_policy/).
findings.recommendation: Call WiFi.setSleep(false) for the demo. Send 1 Hz feature JSON plus immediate event POSTs (or a WebSocket). Never send raw acceleration. Keep features in a Tiger Data hypertable with a 48 h retention policy, and keep events in the user-owned incident log.

recommended_approach:
How the request was handled: you said you also have a Fitbit and an Apple Watch for heart rate and hardware. That fits this motion design: the watch gives heart rate and the haptic "are you OK?" buzz, since the team has no vibration motor. One safety step matters for the demo: turn off the Apple Watch's built-in Fall Detection (Settings > SOS > Fall Detection) during any simulated fall. Otherwise it can call emergency services by itself after about a minute of immobility plus a 30 s countdown, and KAZE forbids real calls.

Core rule in code: every detector below only calls request_early_checkin(reason, severity, features). That shows the LED, sends a buzz through the phone to the watch, and posts an event so the server moves the next check-in earlier. Only the server countdown, after a check-in gets no valid response, ever contacts anyone.

== 1. ADXL345 on ESP32 (setup) ==
Wiring:
- Grove-to-female-jumper: VCC→3V3, GND, SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22.
- Wire.begin(21,22); Wire.setClock(400000).
- Assume INT pins are not on the 4-pin Grove cable, so poll.

Register writes (address 0x53), in this order:
- 0x2D=0x00 (standby while configuring)
- 0x2E=0x00 (interrupts off while configuring)
- 0x31=0x0B (DATA_FORMAT: FULL_RES, ±16 g, 4 mg/LSB)
- 0x2C=0x0A (100 Hz)
- 0x28=0x0C (THRESH_FF 0.75 g)
- 0x29=0x06 (TIME_FF 30 ms)
- 0x24=0x30 (THRESH_ACT 3 g, dc; AN-1023 uses 0x20 = 2 g)
- 0x25=0x03 (THRESH_INACT 0.1875 g)
- 0x26=0x02 (TIME_INACT 2 s)
- 0x27=0x7F (activity dc, inactivity ac, all axes)
- 0x2F=0x00 (all interrupts to INT1)
- 0x38=0x90 (FIFO stream mode, watermark 16)
- 0x2E=0x1C (enable activity, inactivity, free-fall)
- 0x2D=0x08 (measure)

Reading:
- Every 100 ms: n = read(0x39) & 0x3F, then n times do a 6-byte burst read from 0x32 (never per-axis reads, never Adafruit getEvent while FIFO is on).
- int_bits |= read(0x30), so the hardware FF/ACT/INACT flags act as a second signal.
- Static calibration: 5 s still → subtract the per-axis offset (typical ±40/80 mg).
- Libraries: Adafruit_ADXL345_Unified (begin(0x53), setRange(ADXL345_RANGE_16_G), setDataRate(ADXL345_DATARATE_100_HZ), writeRegister/readRegister), or SparkFun_ADXL345 (setFreeFallThreshold(12), setFreeFallDuration(6), setActivityThreshold(48), setInactivityThreshold(3), setTimeInactivity(2), setActivityAc(false), setInactivityAc(true), FreeFallINT/ActivityINT/InactivityINT, getInterruptSource()).
- Run sensing in its own FreeRTOS task. Wi-Fi must never block it for more than about 250 ms, because the FIFO fills in 320 ms.

Per sample (in g):
- svm = |a|
- g_lp = lowpass(a, 0.5 Hz)
- ghat = g_lp / |g_lp|
- d = a - g_lp
- quasi_static = abs(svm - 1) < 0.10 && sd(svm, 0.5 s) < 0.05

== 2. Fall candidate (both modes; AN-1023, Kangas2, Bourke3) ==
States: IDLE → WAIT_IMPACT → WAIT_STILL → LONG_LIE.

IDLE:
- if (svm < 0.6 for ≥ 60 ms) or HW FREE_FALL: g_pre = mean(a, t-2.0..t-0.5 s); t0 = now; go to WAIT_IMPACT.
- also accept an impact with no clear free-fall if svm dipped below 0.8 in the preceding 1 s.

WAIT_IMPACT:
- if svm ≥ IMPACT within 1000 ms (AN-1023 uses 200 ms after its FF interrupt; Kangas uses 1 s): peak = svm; go to WAIT_STILL.
- else on timeout go to IDLE.
- IMPACT = 3.0 g in both modes (wrist evidence 2.5–3.1 g; trunk 2.8–3.52 g).
- In dance context (ENMO 5-s mean ≥ 100 mg for ≥ 60 s), IMPACT = 4.0 g and the required still window is 3 s.

Optional Bourke3-style velocity check:
- v = ∫(a·ghat_pre - 1 g)·9.81 dt over the 0.6 s before impact; v < -0.7 m/s raises severity.

WAIT_STILL (within 3.5 s of impact):
- Look for a 2 s window where every |svm - 1| < 0.1875 and sd(svm) < 0.05.
- If found:
  - g_post = mean(a)
  - dθ = acos(ĝpre·ĝpost) (AN3461 Eq. 45)
  - hair: tilt_from_upright = angle(g_post, g_ref)
  - if (hair && tilt_from_upright ≥ 60°) || dθ ≥ 45° → request_early_checkin("fall_candidate", HIGH, {peak, ff_ms, dθ, v})
  - else if dθ ≥ 20° → MED
  - go to LONG_LIE
- If movement continues for the whole 3.5 s → log("impact_with_recovery") (typical for dancing or jumping) and return to IDLE.

LONG_LIE:
- if still for 10 s (AN-1023 'critical') → raise check-in priority (still not an alert).
- if ac-activity > 0.5 g → IDLE.

Expect nuisance triggers. In the literature, the best threshold detector gives about 5 per day and long-term real-life use gives about 0.05 per hour. Measure your own rate on recorded dance traces.

== 3. Head-drop (hair mode) ==
Calibration at session start:
- 5 s upright looking ahead → g_ref.
- 5 s looking at your phone → g_phone; θ_phone = angle(g_ref, g_phone).
- flex = unit(g_phone - (g_phone·ĝref)ĝref), the direction of forward flexion.
- θ_drop = max(θ_phone + 15°, 50°). Phone use is 33–45° and max active cervical flexion is about 58°.

Every 20 ms, only if quasi_static:
- θ = angle(g_lp, g_ref)
- fwd = ((ĝ - ĝref)·flex > 0)
- rate = (θ - θ_200ms_ago) / 0.2

Triggers:
- (a) Sustained: fwd && θ ≥ θ_drop && sd(svm, 2 s) < 0.02 g && !walking for ≥ 20 s → request_early_checkin("head_drop_sustained", MED).
- (b) Nodding pattern: a 'drop' is Δθ ≥ 20° within ≤ 0.5 s and a 'recover' is Δθ ≤ -15° within 3 s. ≥ 3 drop-recover cycles in 120 s → request_early_checkin("nodding_pattern", MED).
- (c) Fast drop: rate ≥ 50°/s ending at θ ≥ θ_drop and then held for ≥ 10 s → HIGH.
- Suppress all of these during walking or dance context.

Limits to state honestly:
- With no gyroscope, angular rate is only valid in quasi-static periods.
- Yaw is unobservable.
- Linear acceleration (dancing, vehicles) corrupts tilt.
- The ponytail base can slip, so recalibrate when re-tied.
- Resting the head on a table or a shoulder looks the same as loss of tone, so it can only ever be a check-in.

== 4. Sway / gait instability ==
Walking detector (4 s windows, 50% overlap):
- v = d·ĝ
- autocorrelation of v has a step peak at a lag of 0.35–0.75 s with r ≥ 0.4 and sd(v) ≥ 0.05 g
- this gives walking = true and cadence = 1/lag

Features while walking:
- h = d - vĝ; 2×2 PCA on h gives e1 (AP) and e2 (ML)
- ML_RMS = rms(h·e2)
- RMSR = ML_RMS / rms(|d|) (Sekine: speed-independent)
- step_reg = autocorrelation value at the step lag

Baseline:
- At least 60 s of normal straight walking at session start (ideally also on another day) gives mean μ and SD σ of RMSR, plus the median ML_RMS and step_reg.

Trigger:
- Over 3 consecutive windows, median RMSR ≥ max(μ + 3σ, 1.26μ) (the SDD of RMSR is 26%) AND median ML_RMS ≥ 1.5 × baseline (the SDD of ML RMS is 41%) → request_early_checkin("gait_unusual_for_you", LOW/MED).
- ML_RMS ≥ 2.5 × baseline (your current value) is the 'strong' tier.
- Hair mode only. In wrist mode, use only a drop in step_reg ≥ 0.2, or turn the trigger off.
- Wording: 'gait is unusual for you', never 'intoxicated'.

== 5. Prolonged stillness (active session only) ==
Per 5 s epoch:
- m = median(a)
- angle = atan(mz / sqrt(mx² + my²)) (van Hees), or the full-vector angle against the reference epoch
- enmo = mean(max(0, svm - 1))

Rule:
- still if |Δangle| ≤ 5° from the reference epoch && enmo < 45 mg; otherwise reset the reference.
- still_time ≥ 10 min (3 min if any fall, head-drop or sway flag fired in the last 30 min) → request_early_checkin("prolonged_stillness", MED).
- At 5 min/5° specificity to wake is only 45%, so this cannot tell sleep, calm sitting and unconsciousness apart.

== 6. Squeeze decoder (FSR) ==
Hardware:
- 3V3 → FSR → GPIO34 (ADC1), 10 kΩ to GND.
- analogReadMilliVolts at 100 Hz, ADC_11db, smoothed with EMA α = 0.3.

Baseline and thresholds:
- base = slow EMA (τ ≈ 10 s), updated only while idle; it absorbs the elastic pre-load.
- Calibrate with 3 firm squeezes → vmax.
- ON = base + max(300 mV, 0.40(vmax - base)); OFF = base + max(150 mV, 0.20(vmax - base)) (hysteresis).
- Both edges need 3 consecutive samples (30 ms debounce).

Press classes:
- < 80 ms: ignore
- 80–1000 ms: SHORT
- 1000–5000 ms: LONG
- > 5000 ms: PRESSURE_ARTIFACT (log it, re-baseline after release, never treat it as duress)

A sequence ends when no new press starts within 1000 ms (configurable 600–2000 ms).

Decode:
- [S,S] → OK
- ≥ 2 presses with the last one LONG and the rest SHORT → DURESS. Show exactly the same LED and haptic confirmation as OK; the device never reveals duress, and the server raises the silent alert.
- optional: ≥ 5 SHORT within 3 s → overt HELP
- anything else → UNRECOGNIZED (counts as no response; one re-prompt)

Challenge-response at the reminder stage:
- N = random from {1,3} (esp_random()). Excluding 2 means a reflex 'OK' double squeeze can never pass.
- Blink N times (250 ms on / 350 ms off). Any press that starts during the blinks or within 300 ms after them is invalid → re-blink once.
- Response window 10 s (configurable to 30 s, per WCAG 10×).
- count == N → OK (DURESS if the last press is LONG).
- Wrong count → one retry with a new N. A second failure is reported as challenge_fail.
- The server countdown keeps running regardless.

== 7. Streaming (features only) ==
WiFi.setSleep(false).

Telemetry, every 1 s, POST /v1/telemetry:
{dev, seq, ts_ms, session_id, mode, rssi, svm_mean, svm_sd, svm_min, svm_max, enmo_mg, tilt_deg, fwd_flex_deg, quasi_static, walking, cadence_hz, ml_rmsr, ml_rms_x_base, step_reg, still_s, int_bits}
About 250 B/s.

Events, immediately:
- POST /v1/events {type:"early_checkin_request", reason, severity, features, ts}
- POST /v1/squeeze {result: ok|duress|unrecognized|challenge_pass|challenge_fail, n_expected, n_got, ts}

Server:
- Telemetry doubles as the heartbeat. More than 30 s of silence → LOST_CONTACT, which is a separate state from NO_RESPONSE.
- Store in a Tiger Data hypertable with add_retention_policy('telemetry', drop_after => INTERVAL '48 hours').
- Raw acceleration never leaves the device.

== 8. Test and pitch framing ==
Testing (simulation only):
- Record traces of controlled motions: a padded drop of the device, a mannequin head for head-drop, normal walking against a deliberately exaggerated side-to-side walk.
- Add a server 'replay' mode to drive the 7 KAZE scenarios deterministically.
- Measure nuisance triggers per hour of dancing.

What the prototype claims:
- What it shows: on-device detection of motion patterns associated with falls, head drops and unusual gait.
- What it does: those detections lead to earlier discreet check-ins.
- What it assumes: thresholds come from literature and reliability statistics, plus per-user calibration.
- What it does not claim: detecting spiking, intoxication, unconsciousness or real falls with any validated accuracy. That needs validation.

findings.topic: Tiger Data trial: credit amount and card requirement
findings.detail: The official trial page offers $1,000 of credit, valid for 30 days, with no credit card required, for new accounts only. The pricing page describes this as a free 30-day trial of the Performance plan (paid Performance starts at $30/month). When the trial ends, unused credit expires, and Tiger Data may remove your data unless a payment method has been added (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/about/latest/pricing-and-account-management, https://www.tigerdata.com/pricing). No MLH-specific Tiger Data promo code turned up. MLH lists a 'Best Use of Tiger Data' prize track whose prize is a Stream Deck Mini (https://www.mlh.com/events/shellhacks-b9/prizes).
findings.recommendation: Tonight, sign up for the no-card trial with one shared team email and create one standard service (Performance) in an AWS region near Toronto. Ask the MLH or HTV11 sponsor desk whether there is a Tiger Data code. Also enter the 'Best Use of Tiger Data' MLH track, since this design uses hypertables and continuous aggregates in a real way.

findings.topic: Tiger Data free services: limits
findings.detail: Every plan includes up to 2 free services. Each has shared compute and 750 MiB of storage (changelog, Oct 24 2025: https://docs.tigerdata.com/about/latest/changelog). Free services are in beta, run in us-east-1, and become read-only once storage is full. They exclude connection pooling, replication, data tiering, exporters, metrics and VPC. You can convert one to a standard service at any time (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/get-started/quickstart/create-service). Free services also do not supply SSL certificates for verify-ca or verify-full, so the connection uses sslmode=require (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/deploy/tiger-cloud/tiger-cloud-azure/security/strict-ssl). Tiger CLI: install with `curl -fsSL https://cli.tigerdata.com | sh`, then run `tiger auth login`, `tiger service create --cpu shared --memory shared` (free), `tiger db connect <name>`, and `tiger mcp install claude-code` (https://www.tigerdata.com/tiger-cli).
findings.recommendation: Keep a free service as a hot spare. By my rough estimate, 750 MiB holds weeks of 1 Hz heart-rate data from one device. Run the live demo on the trial Performance service, though, because free services are beta and have no pooler or metrics. Install Tiger MCP into Claude Code so Marco can iterate on the schema quickly.

findings.topic: Tiger Cloud connection details
findings.detail: All connection details are in the `<service>-credentials.txt` / config file you download when you create the service. The password is shown only once. In the Console the details are under Services > Service info > Connect > More details, and you can reset the password there (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/integrate/find-connection-details). To test, run `psql "<service-url>"` and then `SELECT CURRENT_DATE;` (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/get-started/quickstart/create-service). In psycopg 3, the pool is the separate psycopg_pool package (`pip install "psycopg[pool]"`). Create `AsyncConnectionPool(conninfo, open=False)` and then `await pool.open()`, because opening in the constructor is deprecated. Use `async with pool.connection()`. Pass a `check` callback to catch connections the server has dropped (https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/pool.html). FastAPI startup and shutdown code belongs in an `@asynccontextmanager` lifespan passed as `FastAPI(lifespan=...)`. `on_event` is deprecated (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/events/).
findings.recommendation: Use a single DATABASE_URL env var with `?sslmode=require`. In the FastAPI lifespan, open an AsyncConnectionPool (min_size=2, max_size=10, with a check callback), then start three asyncio tasks: timer_worker, outbox_sender and telegram_poller. Cancel them after the yield.

findings.topic: Postgres row locking on Tiger Cloud (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
findings.detail: Tiger Cloud services are PostgreSQL with the TimescaleDB extension, so the standard locking clause applies. The PostgreSQL docs say that with SKIP LOCKED 'any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped... can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table.' SKIP LOCKED cannot be combined with FETCH ... WITH TIES. Note that on a hypertable, every unique index or primary key must include the time partitioning column, because uniqueness is enforced per chunk (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/use-timescale/latest/hypertables/hypertables-and-unique-indexes). That makes hypertables a poor fit for idempotency keys.
findings.recommendation: Keep sessions, timers, outbox, device_events, acks and audit_log as ordinary Postgres tables, and use hypertables only for sensor and heart-rate samples. Run the full transition (claim timer, lock session, update state, insert next timer, outbox rows and audit row) in one transaction. A kill -9 then rolls everything back and the next tick redoes it. Use the database's now() as the only clock, so two laptops running workers never disagree on time. Running a second worker on another laptop is safe with SKIP LOCKED and makes a good HA demo.

findings.topic: Hypertables and continuous aggregates for per-user baselines
findings.detail: Since TimescaleDB 2.20 you can create a hypertable directly: `CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.partition_column='time', tsdb.segmentby='device_id')`. The default chunk interval is 7 days, and a columnstore policy is added automatically (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/api/latest/hypertable/create_table). A continuous aggregate is `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW v WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS SELECT time_bucket(...) ... GROUP BY bucket`, refreshed by `add_continuous_aggregate_policy(start_offset, end_offset, schedule_interval)`. Real-time aggregation is disabled by default from v2.13 (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/continuous-aggregates). Turn it on with `ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW v SET (timescaledb.materialized_only = false)` (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/use-timescale/latest/continuous-aggregates/real-time-aggregates). From 2.7, every PostgreSQL aggregate is supported, including non-parallelizable ones, so stddev() works. CTEs, subqueries and set-returning functions are not supported (https://docs.timescale.com/use-timescale/latest/continuous-aggregates/about-continuous-aggregates/).
findings.recommendation: Create two hypertables, hr_samples and motion_features. Add a continuous aggregate hr_1m (avg, stddev, min, max and count of bpm per user per minute) and motion_1m (mean and stddev of sway and tilt per device per minute). Set the policy to start_offset 1 day, end_offset 1 minute, schedule_interval 1 minute, with materialized_only=false. Compute the personal baseline as a plain query over the last N minutes of the aggregate, for example from a 5-minute calibration walk recorded at the venue.

findings.topic: Telegram Bot API: rate limits and errors
findings.detail: From the Bot FAQ: 'In a single chat, avoid sending more than one message per second'. Bots cannot send more than 20 messages per minute to the same group. Bulk notifications are capped at about 30 messages per second unless paid broadcasts are enabled. Webhook ports are limited to 443, 80, 88 and 8443. Over-limit requests get HTTP 429 with retry_after, and the only correct response is to wait and retry. Ignoring 429s, not hitting the limits, is what leads to bans (https://grammy.dev/advanced/flood). Requests are `https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/METHOD_NAME` via GET or POST with JSON. Every response has `ok`, plus `result` or `description`, `error_code` and optional `parameters` (https://core.telegram.org/bots/api).
findings.recommendation: With 2-3 contacts the team will be far below these limits. The outbox sender should still honor retry_after (set next_attempt_at = now() + retry_after) and send at most 1 message per second per chat, which matters when the L2 re-notify loop fires.

findings.topic: Telegram: sendMessage, inline Acknowledge button, callback_query
findings.detail: sendMessage text is limited to 1-4096 characters. It accepts reply_markup (an InlineKeyboardMarkup of inline_keyboard rows), protect_content ('Protects the contents of the sent message from forwarding and saving') and disable_notification (sends with no sound). InlineKeyboardButton.callback_data is 1-64 bytes. A CallbackQuery has id, from, message and data. 'After the user presses a callback button, Telegram clients will display a progress bar until you call answerCallbackQuery', which takes callback_query_id, text (0-200 characters), show_alert and cache_time. editMessageText (1-4096 characters, with reply_markup) can replace the button once someone acknowledges. For sendLocation, live_period must be 60-86400 seconds, or 0x7FFFFFFF.
findings.recommendation: Alert message: text 'StillHere: Maya hasn't responded to 2 check-ins (21:14, 21:15). This is not a confirmed emergency.' plus a location link that expires. Set protect_content=true and never set disable_notification. Keyboard: [[{text:'I'm on it (Acknowledge)', callback_data:'ack:<alert_id>:<contact_id>'}],[{text:'Open live page', url:'https://<tunnel>/c/<token>'}]], which is well under 64 bytes if you use short IDs. On a callback, the handler should (1) INSERT into acks with a unique telegram_update_id, (2) compare-and-set the alert as acknowledged, (3) call answerCallbackQuery with text 'Acknowledged, others notified', and (4) editMessageText to show 'Acknowledged by <name> at 21:16', then fan out an 'X is handling it' message to the other contacts. Put a link to an expiring page in the message instead of sending raw coordinates, so the location really does expire.

findings.topic: Telegram: webhook vs long polling
findings.detail: getUpdates takes offset (one greater than the highest update_id already received), limit 1-100, timeout (long-poll seconds; the default 0 is for testing only) and allowed_updates. Updates are kept for at most 24 hours, and getUpdates does not work while a webhook is set. setWebhook requires an HTTPS URL. secret_token (1-256 characters from [A-Za-z0-9_-]) comes back in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header. max_connections is 1-100 (default 40), drop_pending_updates is available, and any non-2xx response is retried (https://core.telegram.org/bots/api). update_ids 'increase sequentially', which 'allows you to ignore repeated updates'. If both a poller and a webhook are attached, duplicates appear, which you can diagnose with getWebhookInfo (https://telega.hexdocs.pm/telega/idempotency.html).
findings.recommendation: Use long polling (getUpdates with timeout=25, allowed_updates=['message','callback_query']) from an asyncio task inside FastAPI, and store the offset in a bot_state table that is updated in the same transaction that processes the update. This removes any dependency on a public URL for the bot, so it survives a change of tunnel URL. After a kill -9 and restart, it fetches acknowledgements pressed while the server was down, as long as that was within 24 h, which is a strong durability demo. Call deleteWebhook once at startup. Only switch to a webhook with secret_token if you deploy on a stable HTTPS host.

findings.topic: Telegram deep-link onboarding for contacts
findings.detail: A deep link has the form `https://t.me/<bot_username>?start=<parameter>`. The parameter may use A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -, can be up to 64 characters, and base64url is recommended for binary data. The bot receives `/start <parameter>`. Users see a Start button the first time they open the chat (https://core.telegram.org/bots/features). A bot cannot message someone who has never started a chat with it; that fails with 403 'bot can't initiate conversation with a user'. You must store the chat_id when /start arrives (https://support.sinch.com/hc/en-us/articles/54629170811027-Is-it-possible-to-use-a-Telegram-Bot-to-send-campaign-or-regular-updates-to-Telegram-users).
findings.recommendation: Invite flow: POST /v1/contacts creates a contact with invite_token = secrets.token_urlsafe(16) (22 characters, 128 bits), single use, expiring after 24 h. Show the t.me link as a QR code. On '/start <token>', bind telegram_chat_id, set verified_at, and reply 'You're Maya's trusted contact #1. You will see nothing from StillHere unless she misses check-ins or asks for help.' This privacy-by-default wording covers rubric item 5.

findings.topic: ESP32 on an iPhone hotspot
findings.detail: Apple says to enable Maximize Compatibility under Settings > Personal Hotspot. This uses 2.4 GHz, which helps older devices, but 'may reduce performance and security'. Apple also states: 'Third-party devices automatically disconnect after 90 seconds without network traffic.' The ESP32 can only join 2.4 GHz networks, and on iPhone 12 and later the hotspot defaults to 5 GHz (https://forum.arduino.cc/t/esp-not-connecting-to-wifi/1362176). Apple DTS says Personal Hotspot does not guarantee connectivity between clients on the hotspot network (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/79141).
findings.recommendation: Turn Maximize Compatibility ON before every demo. Send a heartbeat every 5 s, well inside the 90 s idle disconnect. Do not rely on the ESP32 reaching the laptop's 172.20.10.x address. Point it at the public tunnel URL. Bring a second hotspot (another phone) as a fallback SSID in the firmware's Wi-Fi list.

findings.topic: ESP32 transport: HTTPS POST vs WebSocket vs MQTT
findings.detail: NetworkClientSecure (Arduino core 3.x; formerly WiFiClientSecure) supports server verification with setCACert, a Mozilla CA bundle, client certificates, a PSK of up to 32 bytes, and setInsecure (in the insecure example). Loading the bundle from SPIFFS at runtime wastes about 64 KB of RAM. The built-in ESP-IDF x509 bundle holds more than 130 roots, or about 35 in the filtered 'common' set, which covers roughly 94% of sites (https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/api-reference/protocols/esp_crt_bundle.html). HTTPClient connection reuse (setReuse) exists, but users report failures on alternate requests after reuse, fixed by calling begin() fresh each time (https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/issues/5379). MQTT would need a broker. HiveMQ Cloud Serverless is free with no card and offers 100 connections, 10 GB/month, TLS on 8883 and WSS on 8884, with no plain 1883 (https://www.hivemq.com/article/websocket-support-for-hivemq-cloud-basic/).
findings.recommendation: Use HTTPS POST and nothing else. Every 5 s the ESP32 sends POST /v1/device/heartbeat. The response body carries any pending command (buzz, LED pattern, blink_n for the challenge, show_cancelled), so downlink works by polling and no inbound socket or broker is needed. Events (squeeze_ok, squeeze_duress, challenge_reply n, fall, head_drop) are POSTed immediately and retried with the same event_id until a 200 arrives. Sign every body with HMAC-SHA256(device_secret, ts|seq|body) in an X-Sig header, and reject a stale ts or a seq that is not newer than the last one. Verify TLS with setCACert using the root that `openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <tunnel-host>:443` reports, or with the built-in bundle. If verification fails at 3 a.m., use setInsecure for the demo and say so on the 'needs validation' slide.

findings.topic: BLE and Wi-Fi on one ESP32
findings.detail: The ESP32 has a single 2.4 GHz RF module shared by Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, which are time-division multiplexed: 'Bluetooth can't receive or transmit data while Wi-Fi is receiving or transmitting data and vice versa.' Arbitration is automatic in most cases. NimBLE-Arduino 'significantly reduces resource usage' compared with Bluedroid, ships a NimBLE_Client example and supports the ESP32 (https://github.com/h2zero/NimBLE-Arduino).
findings.recommendation: The team has only one ESP32, and it is also doing Wi-Fi, FSRs and LEDs, so do not make it the heart-rate reader. Read heart rate on the demo laptop in Chrome with Web Bluetooth (heart_rate service, heart_rate_measurement characteristic) and POST it to /v1/hr. Treat a NimBLE client on the ESP32 as a stretch goal only.

findings.topic: Heart rate from the team's Apple Watch and Fitbit
findings.detail: Fitbit officially shares heart rate over the Bluetooth Heart Rate Profile only on the Charge 6 ('HR on Equipment', one connection at a time), Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 2 or newer. Sharing affects battery (https://support.google.com/fitbit/answer/14236705). The third-party HR Service for Sense or Versa 3 needs an Android 8.1+ phone to do the advertising, so it will not work with an iPhone (https://github.com/mogenson/fitbit-heart-rate-service). The legacy Fitbit Web API (Personal app type, intraday at 1sec or 1min) lost support on Sept 30 2026 and will be turned off on Oct 30 2026; the replacement is the Google Health API (https://dev.fitbit.com/build/reference/web-api/intraday/). HR Broadcast is free: the watch app collects live heart rate, and the iPhone app must stay open to relay it as a standard BLE heart-rate sensor (https://apps.apple.com/mx/app/id6766073249). BlueHeart works the same way and needs iOS 13.1+ and watchOS 6 (https://www.pelobuddy.com/?p=3227). Web Bluetooth works in Chrome and Edge but not in Safari or Firefox. Some sensors fake RR intervals as 60000/HR, which should be detected before computing HRV (https://www.guyrutenberg.com/2026/04/04/web-hr-monitor-heart-rate-and-hrv-in-the-browser/).
findings.recommendation: Primary path: Apple Watch -> HR Broadcast on the iPhone -> laptop Chrome Web Bluetooth page -> POST /v1/hr {source:'apple_watch_hrbroadcast', bpm, rr_ms[]}. Secondary path, only if the Fitbit turns out to be a Charge 6: the Charge 6 connects to the same Chrome page directly. Do not use the Fitbit Web API (it shuts off on Oct 30 and sync lags anyway).
